title: QOSMIC's ARGUS Patent: Bengaluru Startup Wins US Patent for Laser-Communication Ground Station
excerpt: QOSMIC Satellite Systems won a US patent on September 8 for ARGUS, a multi-aperture optical ground station for satellite laser communications — technology the startup says was conceived, engineered and validated in India.
body:
• QOSMIC Satellite Systems, a Bengaluru deep-tech startup incubated at ARTPARK in IISc, has secured a US patent for ARGUS — its optical ground station designed to receive high-speed laser communications from satellites. The patent was granted on September 8, 2026, India Today reported.
  • ARGUS replaces a single giant telescope with multiple smaller telescope units working together as one receiving system. Units can be added to expand capacity, and collected signals are sent to a central processing unit producing what the company describes as "a signal equivalent to that of a much larger telescope."
  • The startup says it filed the application in April and received the grant in under a year — with the technology conceived, engineered and validated in India — a marker of Indian deep-tech intellectual property moving at global speed.
  • The company, backed by Accel, Prosus, South Park Commons and ARTPARK, is also developing ZAPHOD, a satellite optical terminal, as laser links emerge to relieve bandwidth limits on traditional radio-frequency satellite communications.

QOSMIC Satellite Systems, a deep-tech startup based in Bengaluru, has won a United States patent for the architecture behind ARGUS, its optical ground station built to receive high-speed laser communications from satellites in orbit. The patent was granted on September 8, 2026, according to a September 15 report by India Today's Science Desk — a milestone that puts a young Indian company on the global map of optical satellite-communications infrastructure.

QOSMIC filed the patent application in April and received the grant in under a year, the company said. Rather than building its own satellites, QOSMIC develops the underlying systems that let them communicate — electronics, hardware and architectures for optical ground stations that capture laser signals beamed down from space.

What ARGUS does differently

The core of the patented design is a multi-aperture approach. Traditional optical ground stations rely on a single large telescope to catch faint laser signals from orbit. ARGUS instead combines multiple smaller telescope units into one unified receiving system, capturing and combining satellite laser transmissions with greater efficiency and resilience.

The design is expandable — capacity grows by adding more telescope units rather than building a bigger dish. It incorporates precision optics, adjustable telescope mounts, angular positioning and vibration isolation, with the collected optical signals redirected to a central processing unit. The result, QOSMIC says, is "a signal equivalent to that of a much larger telescope" — without the cost and engineering complexity of a single giant mirror.

"The result, QOSMIC says, is "a signal equivalent to that of a much larger telescope" — without the cost and engineering complexity of a single giant mirror."

The patent sits alongside the company's other work on ZAPHOD, its satellite optical terminal — the other end of the laser link. Together they position QOSMIC as a full-stack player in optical satellite communications: terminals in space and the ground stations that talk to them.

Why laser communication matters now

Most satellite communication today runs on radio frequencies, which face growing congestion and hard physical limits on data rates. As constellations multiply and satellite data volumes surge — from Earth observation and navigation to broadband services — laser communication offers a path to far higher bandwidth, lower spectrum congestion and more efficient links.

Space agencies and private companies worldwide are racing to build the ground infrastructure for that shift. Optical ground stations are the land-based half of the equation: without them, laser-linked satellites cannot deliver their data. A patented, modular, Indian-designed ground station is exactly the kind of infrastructure the sector needs as it scales.

An Indian IP milestone

QOSMIC was founded and incubated at ARTPARK, the robotics and AI innovation hub at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru, and counts Accel, Prosus, South Park Commons and ARTPARK among its backers. The company stresses that ARGUS was conceived, engineered and validated in India — and is now protected in the United States, the world's most commercially important IP jurisdiction for deep tech.

The grant fits a pattern. Last month, Bengaluru's GalaxEye secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR satellite imaging system — the first US patent for an Indian startup in satellite imaging — and is flying its Mission Drishti satellite. Together, the two patents mark a shift in India's private space sector: from building services around imported technology to inventing foundational infrastructure and protecting it globally.

India's private space industry has expanded rapidly since the sector opened to private participation, with policy support through IN-SPACe and a growing pipeline of startups working on launch vehicles, satellite platforms and Earth-observation payloads. Ground infrastructure has been a quieter corner of that boom — and one where a patented, scalable design could travel well beyond India's borders.

Why it matters for the diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, milestones like this are about more than one startup. Bengaluru's deep-tech ecosystem — fed by IISc, research labs and a dense network of returning engineers — is producing intellectual property that competes at the frontier of space communications. NRIs in aerospace, semiconductors and venture capital are increasingly part of that loop, as investors, collaborators and talent. A US patent granted in under a year for technology invented in India is the kind of signal that pulls that loop tighter.

What's next

The patent gives QOSMIC enforceable protection for its ground-station architecture in the US market, strengthening its position as it commercialises. Watch for deployment of ARGUS stations, progress on the ZAPHOD optical terminal, and whether other Indian startups follow the QOSMIC–GalaxEye playbook: invent in India, patent in the United States, and sell to a global market.
